source.name: JPL Small-Body Database API, 109P/Swift-Tuttle; osculating elements, equinox J2000, ecliptic plane

radius.source: JPL Small-Body Database physical parameters for 109P: nucleus diameter 26 km (Lamy et al. 2004, Comets II, pp. 223-264: Lamy, Toth, Fernandez and Weaver), half of it; JPL Horizons comet header for 109P prints RAD = 13 km (both read 2026-10-15). A comet has no gravitational parameter in either source, so it cannot be a two-body centre.

accuracy.statement: Position was compared with JPL Horizons at eight dates from 1990 to 2030: the largest Sun-centred difference is about 10,686,093 km (0.86% of its distance from the Sun at that date), so this is an approximate position for drawing the orbit and the comet's place on it, not an ephemeris. This is the largest difference at the eight dates compared, not a bound for every date. Compared with JPL Horizons, target DES=109P;CAP (solution JPL#32), centre 500@10, ICRF.
limitations: The elements are a fit to the 1737-1995 observations.
Horizons applies perturbations from a fit to the same observations, so the two drift apart.
Positions before 1990 or after 2030 were not compared with Horizons; the orbit reaches 51 AU and takes 133 years, a long span for two-body motion.
The comet's size is the nucleus alone (a 26 km body); the coma and tail are not modelled. No velocity or orientation is modelled.

source.name: NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, 109P/Swift-Tuttle, solution SB405-CPV-2 (equinox J2000, epoch JD 2450000.5); sizes the whole-orbit path's sampling, the comet's position is the two-body source built from parentElements
Global Meteor Network, monthly trajectory summary files (traj_summary_monthly_YYYYMM.txt), IAU shower 7 (PER); Vida et al. 2021, MNRAS 506(4); Vida et al. 2020, MNRAS 491(2)

gmn.ruleNote: Qc is GMN's own maximum convergence angle between stations (column Qc, deg) and the Vgeo sigma is the uncertainty column beside Vgeo (km/s), so the reliable set is Qc at least the angle and sigma at most the fraction of Vgeo.

rule.quote: "requiring a minimum convergence angle of 15 degrees between cameras, ensuring an estimated velocity error of no more than 10% of the nominal value" (the 2025 HDBSCAN paper words it: "a minimum convergence angle of 15° between camera detections to ensure reliable triangulation, ... a velocity error not exceeding 10% of the nominal value"); both apply it to the CAMS v3.0 database; they also drop hyperbolic orbits, which the data file already does

source.name: Peña-Asensio and Sánchez-Lozano 2024, Statistical Equivalence of Metrics for Meteor Dynamical Association, Advances in Space Research, doi 10.1016/j.asr.2024.05.005 (arXiv 2405.03308); and arXiv 2507.01501, Meteoroid stream identification with HDBSCAN

concentration.basis: not a published fit. 20 degrees of mean anomaly either side is about 15 years of the 133-year orbit. Young dust is known to crowd near the parent (the early-1990s Perseid outbursts followed the comet's 1992 return), but no published fraction or width is claimed.

source.name: International Meteor Organization, 2020 Meteor Shower Calendar (ed. J. Rendtel), the Perseids entry: active July 17 - August 24, maximum August 12, 13h to 16h UT; archived copy
source.note: The peak rate is 100 meteors per hour (ZHR), the American Meteor Society calendar figure; the IMO entry gives 110. The peak instant is when the Sun reaches the IAU Meteor Data Center peak solar longitude of 140.1 degrees, which falls inside the IMO's 13h to 16h UT maximum. The rate curve falls off from that instant.

source.name: IAU Meteor Data Center, established meteor showers, Perseids (PER, 7), parameter set AdNo 9 (Jenniskens 2023, Atlas of Earth's Meteor Showers): peak solar longitude 140.1 deg, geocentric radiant RA 47.9, Dec +57.9 deg, J2000
